transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess it’s work. I’m a barber, and it’s gotten to this point where I’ll do almost anything to not use the straight razor. Like I’ll switch clients with someone, or say the blade’s missing, or just hide it in the drawer, which sounds ridiculous when I say it out loud.

And I mean, the shop is busy, there’s always music on, guys talking about basketball or whatever, so sometimes I can kind of cover it. But if I can’t get out of doing the shave, I’m shaking through the whole thing. That’s basically why I’m here.
When you have to use the straight razor, do you get unwanted thoughts that you might accidentally cut or seriously hurt the client?

Yeah… that’s pretty much it. I know, logically, it’s just a tool. I trained with it, and I can use clippers all day without even thinking about it—like I’m fine doing fades, lineups, all that.

But when the straight razor is open at my station, it’s like my brain jumps straight to, “I’m going to cut this guy,” or cut myself badly. And then I start thinking about how close it is to someone’s neck, which is stupid because that’s literally the job, you know? But it feels like something bad is about to happen.
When that thought comes up, does it feel like an unwanted thought popping into your mind, even though you don’t want to hurt anyone?

Yeah, yeah, it’s unwanted. I mean, I don’t want to hurt anybody—obviously. I cut hair because I like making people look good, you know? Some guys come in before weddings or job interviews, and they’re trusting you, and then my head goes off somewhere else.

But yeah, when that straight razor is open at my station, even though I know it’s just a tool I trained with, it suddenly feels like I’m about to cut the client badly or even cut myself. Clippers don’t do that to me at all. It’s just that razor.
When that thought shows up, does it feel intrusive and against what you want, like it pops into your mind even though you don’t want it there?

I mean… I think so? It’s hard to explain. It’s not like I’m standing there planning anything, if that’s what you mean. It just kind of jumps in, and then I get stuck on it.

Like, even yesterday, this guy was talking to me about his kid’s soccer game while I was doing his neck cleanup, and I’m supposed to be listening, but then I’m suddenly thinking about the razor and how sharp it is, and then I’m not really hearing him anymore. Which is awkward because customers can tell when you’re not paying attention.

So yeah, I guess it feels like it pops in when I don’t want it to. I don’t know if “intrusive” is the right word, but it’s definitely not something I’m trying to think about.
When that fear comes up, do you find yourself repeatedly checking the razor to make sure it’s safe?

Um… checking it repeatedly? I don’t know. I mean, I look at it, obviously, because I have to use it and make sure it’s set up right, but I don’t know if I’d call it checking over and over to make sure it’s safe.

Sometimes I’ll kind of stare at it longer than I need to, like I’m trying to convince myself it’s just a razor, you know? But then I’ll get distracted thinking about how old-school barbers used to use these things all day like it was nothing—my uncle used to talk about that, actually, he had this whole thing about “real barbering” and keeping the blade angle right.

Sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess… I haven’t really noticed myself repeatedly checking it in a specific way. It’s more that once I see it, I get tense about using it.
Do you only get this fear when the straight razor is there in front of you?

Not only when it’s right in front of me, no. Like, the second a client asks for a razor shave, I already feel it start—my chest tightens up, my hands get sweaty, and it’s like my body wants to step back before I’ve even done anything.

And then if I actually see the blade flipped open, it’s worse. Which is annoying, because some clients ask for it like it’s this classic barber thing, you know, like they’ve seen it in movies or those fancy shops with the hot towels and everything. I used to think that part of the job was kind of cool, honestly.

But now, yeah, even hearing them ask can set it off.
When that thought about cutting someone comes up, do you do anything on purpose to make the thought go away or feel less dangerous?

I’m not totally sure. Like, I don’t have a specific thing I do in my head, if that’s what you mean. I don’t say a phrase or count or anything like that.

Sometimes I’ll try to focus really hard on the actual steps, like the angle and where my hand is supposed to be, because that’s what they drilled into us when I was learning. My instructor used to make this big deal about posture too, like your elbow position mattered more than people think—sorry, that’s probably not what you asked.

I guess I just try to push it away or focus on the job, but I don’t know if I’m doing something on purpose to make it “less dangerous.” It’s more like I’m uncomfortable and I’m trying to get through the moment.
When this happens at work, are you mainly afraid that other people will notice you seem anxious or think badly of you?

I don’t think that’s the main thing, no. I mean, I don’t love the idea of looking nervous in front of a client, obviously—barbering is such a face-to-face job, and people notice your hands, your confidence, the whole vibe of the shop.

But… I don’t know, when it happens, I’m not mostly thinking, “They’re going to judge me.” It’s more just the situation itself gets in my head. Like the razor and what I’m doing with it.

Though sometimes I do wonder if they can tell I’m tense, especially if the shop is quiet. My old boss used to say clients can feel when you’re not relaxed—he had all these sayings about “the chair being a stage” and stuff. Sorry, I’m wandering. But no, I don’t think it’s mainly about people thinking badly of me.
Do you feel that your fear about using the straight razor is excessive or unreasonable?

Yeah… I mean, part of me knows it’s excessive. I trained with straight razors, it’s literally just one of the tools of the trade. I can use clippers all day, scissors, trimmers, no problem—half the time I’m not even thinking about it.

But when that straight razor is sitting there open at my station, it doesn’t feel like “just a tool.” It feels like I’m about to hurt somebody, or like I’m going to cut myself badly. And I know that probably sounds dramatic, because barbers use them every day, but in the moment it feels really real.
Outside of using or thinking about the straight razor at work, do you also find yourself worrying a lot about many other things in your life?

Um… not really, I don’t think so. I mean, I worry about normal stuff, like whether a client’s going to like the cut, or bills, or if I’m running late—normal life stuff.

But it’s not like my brain is constantly jumping from one worry to the next all day. It’s more tied to the razor thing. Like if I’m not at work or not thinking about using it, I’m usually not sitting around worrying about a bunch of other things.

Although sometimes work in general gets in my head—like the shop atmosphere, keeping your station clean, people watching you cut hair. There was this one guy I used to work with who could talk nonstop while doing a fade perfectly, and I was always like, how do you even do that? Sorry, that’s not really what you asked.

So… no, I wouldn’t say I worry a lot about many other things. Mostly it’s that specific situation.
Are you afraid you might lose control and intentionally hurt a client with the straight razor?

No… I don’t think it’s like I’m afraid I’ll choose to do something on purpose. It’s not that I want to hurt anyone or that I think I’m going to suddenly decide to.

It’s more like, when the straight razor is open there on my station, my brain just goes straight to, “What if I hurt them?” or “What if I cut myself badly?” Even though I know I trained with it, and I can use clippers all day without even thinking. It’s just that razor—seeing it open makes the whole thing feel dangerous in a way I know doesn’t totally make sense.
When you avoid using the straight razor, does that make your fear go down right away?

Yeah… honestly, yes. Like, if I find a way not to use it, I feel relief pretty much right away. I’ll switch clients if I can, or say the blade’s missing, or just kind of keep it tucked away in the drawer and hope nobody asks for a shave.

It’s embarrassing, because it’s part of the job, you know? In barber school they make it seem like this classic skill, and some guys act like it’s the whole identity of being a barber—hot towel, straight razor, the whole thing. I used to think that looked really cool, actually.

But now, if I avoid it, my body calms down fast. And if I can’t get out of it, I’m just… shaking through the whole shave, trying to look normal.
Are you mainly afraid of the straight razor itself?

Yeah… mainly the straight razor itself, I guess. Like, I know it’s just a tool, and I trained with it. It’s not like I’m scared of every sharp thing—I mean, I use clippers all day, scissors too, and that’s fine.

But when that straight razor is sitting open at my station… it just changes. My brain goes, like, “What if I hurt somebody?” or “What if I cut myself really badly?” Even if nothing is happening yet.

It’s weird because some barbers make it look so smooth, like it’s this elegant old-school thing, and I used to think that was kind of cool. But for me now, once it’s open, it feels dangerous in a way I can’t shake.
Do thoughts about accidentally cutting someone ever come into your mind when you’re away from the straight razor?

I’m not totally sure… I mean, not really in the same way, I don’t think.

Like if I’m at home making food and I see a knife, I don’t usually spiral about a client or anything. Although I did cut myself once chopping onions, but that was just me being stupid and rushing, not like… the barber thing.

It’s more tied to the shop, I guess, and that razor being there. But I don’t know, sometimes if I know I have a client coming in who might ask for a shave, I’ll start thinking about it before they even get there. So… away from the actual razor? Maybe a little if I’m anticipating it, but it’s not like I’m walking around all day thinking about cutting people.
When the thought comes up that you might cut someone, do you mentally replay the shave steps to reassure yourself?

Um… mentally replay the steps? I don’t know if I do it like that exactly.

Like, I’ll think, “Okay, don’t mess up, keep your hand steady,” but I’m not sure I’m going through the whole shave in my head like a checklist or anything. Barber school drilled those steps into us so much—stretch the skin, angle the blade, light pressure—and our instructor used to walk around correcting everybody like a drill sergeant. He had this old mustache too, kind of like one of those 1920s barbershop posters…

Sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed myself doing a full mental replay to feel better. It’s more just the fear pops up and I’m trying to get through it or avoid it.
When you’re holding the straight razor, do you ever get a sudden unwanted image or urge of slashing or intentionally hurting the client?

I… I don’t think so? Not like an urge, no. That sounds… I don’t know, really scary to even say.

When I’m holding it, my head is more like, “Don’t slip, don’t mess this up,” and then I notice my hand or the angle, or the client moving a tiny bit. Like some guys talk the whole time in the chair, you know, and they’ll turn their head while they’re telling you about their weekend, and I’m like, please just stay still for two seconds.

But an image of me slashing someone on purpose… I haven’t noticed that. It’s more just fear something could go wrong, if that makes sense.

doctor.question: When you avoid using the straight razor, does that make your fear go down right away?

target_item.name: Phobic_Avoidance_Endure
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because I’ve gotten to where I’ll do almost anything to avoid using the straight razor at work—switch clients, say the blade’s missing, hide it in the drawer—and if I can’t get out of it, I’m shaking through the whole shave.
target_item.reason: The question is directly about what happens when avoiding the straight razor, which relates to active avoidance of the phobic situation.

patient.answer:
Yeah… honestly, yes. Like, if I find a way not to use it, I feel relief pretty much right away. I’ll switch clients if I can, or say the blade’s missing, or just kind of keep it tucked away in the drawer and hope nobody asks for a shave.

It’s embarrassing, because it’s part of the job, you know? In barber school they make it seem like this classic skill, and some guys act like it’s the whole identity of being a barber—hot towel, straight razor, the whole thing. I used to think that looked really cool, actually.

But now, if I avoid it, my body calms down fast. And if I can’t get out of it, I’m just… shaking through the whole shave, trying to look normal.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a specific phobia from OCD by determining whether the fear is centered on the razor itself as a dangerous object rather than on intrusive harm obsessions.
doctor.question: Are you mainly afraid of the straight razor itself?

target_item.name: Specific_Phobic_Fear
target_item.manifestation: I know it’s just a tool I trained with and I can use clippers all day, but when that straight razor is sitting open at my station it feels like I’m about to hurt somebody or cut myself badly.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the fear is focused on the specific phobic object, the straight razor itself.

patient.answer:
Yeah… mainly the straight razor itself, I guess. Like, I know it’s just a tool, and I trained with it. It’s not like I’m scared of every sharp thing—I mean, I use clippers all day, scissors too, and that’s fine.

But when that straight razor is sitting open at my station… it just changes. My brain goes, like, “What if I hurt somebody?” or “What if I cut myself really badly?” Even if nothing is happening yet.

It’s weird because some barbers make it look so smooth, like it’s this elegant old-school thing, and I used to think that was kind of cool. But for me now, once it’s open, it feels dangerous in a way I can’t shake.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the core fear is of accidental harm from a specific object/situation (supporting specific phobia) versus recurrent intrusive harm obsessions not limited to exposure to the object (supporting OCD).
doctor.question: Do thoughts about accidentally cutting someone ever come into your mind when you’re away from the straight razor?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether accidental-cutting thoughts occur when away from the straight razor, which is not covered by the listed symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
I’m not totally sure… I mean, not really in the same way, I don’t think.

Like if I’m at home making food and I see a knife, I don’t usually spiral about a client or anything. Although I did cut myself once chopping onions, but that was just me being stupid and rushing, not like… the barber thing.

It’s more tied to the shop, I guess, and that razor being there. But I don’t know, sometimes if I know I have a client coming in who might ask for a shave, I’ll start thinking about it before they even get there. So… away from the actual razor? Maybe a little if I’m anticipating it, but it’s not like I’m walking around all day thinking about cutting people.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a specific phobia of the straight razor from OCD by determining whether the patient engages in covert neutralizing/reassurance rituals after the intrusive harm thought.
doctor.question: When the thought comes up that you might cut someone, do you mentally replay the shave steps to reassure yourself?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a mental reassurance behavior, like replaying steps to neutralize or check the thought, which is not covered by the listed specific phobia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
Um… mentally replay the steps? I don’t know if I do it like that exactly.

Like, I’ll think, “Okay, don’t mess up, keep your hand steady,” but I’m not sure I’m going through the whole shave in my head like a checklist or anything. Barber school drilled those steps into us so much—stretch the skin, angle the blade, light pressure—and our instructor used to walk around correcting everybody like a drill sergeant. He had this old mustache too, kind of like one of those 1920s barbershop posters…

Sorry, I’m getting off track. I guess I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed myself doing a full mental replay to feel better. It’s more just the fear pops up and I’m trying to get through it or avoid it.

doctor.intent: Differentiate a specific phobia of the straight razor from OCD by testing whether the fear includes classic ego-dystonic intrusive urges/images of intentionally harming the client.
doctor.question: When you’re holding the straight razor, do you ever get a sudden unwanted image or urge of slashing or intentionally hurting the client?

target_item.reason: The question is specifically about sudden unwanted intrusive images or urges of intentionally harming the client, which is not covered by the listed specific phobia symptom profile items.

patient.answer:
I… I don’t think so? Not like an urge, no. That sounds… I don’t know, really scary to even say.

When I’m holding it, my head is more like, “Don’t slip, don’t mess this up,” and then I notice my hand or the angle, or the client moving a tiny bit. Like some guys talk the whole time in the chair, you know, and they’ll turn their head while they’re telling you about their weekend, and I’m like, please just stay still for two seconds.

But an image of me slashing someone on purpose… I haven’t noticed that. It’s more just fear something could go wrong, if that makes sense.

inference.note: Fear is circumscribed to the straight razor, triggered by anticipation/exposure, recognized as excessive, and relieved by avoidance. Repeated checking, rituals, broader obsessions, and ego-dystonic aggressive urges/images are not supported, making OCD less likely.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking care today
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a marked, circumscribed fear centered on the straight razor, with immediate anxiety on anticipation or exposure, clear avoidance, rapid relief after avoidance, recognition that the fear is excessive, and impairment in occupational functioning. The fear is not primarily about social evaluation, generalized worry, or intentional violent impulses, and there is insufficient evidence for OCD compulsions or broader obsessions. This is most consistent with specific phobia, other type.
